passage:
Thursday. Rekha Ma'am brought a police officer to our class today. I hid behind Arjun because Dadi always says, "Behave or the police will take you away." My legs went funny.
But the officer said her job is to help. She said if you get lost, find someone in uniform, say your name and your parents' phone number, and stay put. She made us say ours three times. I asked, "Do you take naughty children?" She laughed and said, "No, I help find their mummies."
I am still a bit scared of the whistle. But I know my number now. I will say it loud and polite.
Sachin

qa.q: Who brought the police officer to class?
qa.a: Rekha Ma'am brought the police officer.

qa.q: What was Sachin feeling when hiding behind Arjun?
qa.a: Sachin was scared, because Dadi always says the police will take naughty children away, and Sachin's legs went funny.

qa.q: What will Sachin do if lost, after the officer's talk?
qa.a: Sachin will find someone in uniform, say the name and parents' phone number loudly and politely, and stay put.

qa.q: How might the officer have seen Sachin's question about naughty children?
qa.a: The officer laughed and answered kindly, so she probably understood that children can be frightened of the uniform and wanted to reassure Sachin.

grounding: A child who fears the police because adults said they take you away learns that police help, and to be cautious yet respectful.

passage:
At the temple fair, Anjali, eight, let go of her mother Bhavna's hand to watch a puppet show. When the crowd moved, she was alone among strangers' legs. Bhavna always said, "Behave, or the police will take you." Now Anjali saw a constable near the bus stand with a stiff cap and a whistle, and her knees shook.
Then she remembered the school talk: find someone in uniform, say your name and number. She walked up with folded hands. "Namaste. I am lost. I am Anjali. My mother is Bhavna. Papa's number is..."
The constable crouched and dialled. In a few minutes Bhavna came running. Later she said, "I should not have said that about the police."

qa.q: Who did Anjali find near the bus stand?
qa.a: Anjali found a constable near the bus stand.

qa.q: What was Anjali feeling as she saw the constable?
qa.a: Anjali felt frightened, with shaking knees, because her mother had always said the police would take her.

qa.q: What choice did Anjali make that got her back to her mother?
qa.a: She remembered the school talk and walked up to the constable, said her name and number politely, and the constable dialled.

qa.q: Why might Bhavna have said she should not have talked about the police that way?
qa.a: Bhavna saw that the fear she had put in Anjali nearly stopped Anjali from asking for help, and wanted to change it.

grounding: A child sees police as scary because adults said they take you away, and learns that police are there to help, staying cautious yet respectful.

passage:
Class teacher's note, Class 2, road-safety day.
When the traffic constable walked in, Afreen, seven, burst into tears and hid under her desk. Her friend Payal crouched beside her.
Afreen sobbed, "My chachi says police take away bad children!"
The constable took off his cap and sat on a small chair. He said, "I'm here to help children cross roads safely. I don't take children away for being naughty." He let Payal blow his whistle.
Afreen peeked out. Slowly, she came to sit on the mat.
I told the class that police help people, and that if they are ever lost, they can go to a police officer, calmly and politely.
Next step: I'll tell Afreen's mother so they can talk at home.

qa.q: What did the constable let Payal do?
qa.a: He let Payal blow his whistle.

qa.q: Why did Afreen hide under her desk?
qa.a: Afreen felt terrified because her chachi had told her police take away bad children.

qa.q: What did the constable and the teacher do that helped?
qa.a: The constable removed his cap, sat down and explained he helps children, and the teacher told the class police are there to help, to approach calmly and politely.

qa.q: How might Payal see the constable's visit?
qa.a: Payal seemed curious and unafraid, happily blowing the whistle and comforting her friend.

grounding: A child told that police take away naughty children is terrified of a constable, and a calm explanation that police are there to help eases her fear.

passage:
Dear Diary,
Today was the scariest and best day.
Uday's little dog, Toffee, ran out of the park into the market. We ran after him and got lost.
Then I saw a policeman. My Nani always says, "If you're naughty, the police will catch you." My legs shook. I wanted to run away.
But Uday said, "Farhan, Ammi told me police help lost people." So we went to him, very slowly, and said, "Sir, our dog is lost and we are also lost."
He laughed kindly, radioed someone and walked us back. On the way we found Toffee eating a samosa!
He told us, "If you're lost, come to us. Be polite. We help."
Now I don't think police are scary. Just careful.
Farhan

qa.q: What was the name of Uday's dog?
qa.a: The dog was called Toffee.

qa.q: How did Farhan feel when he first saw the policeman?
qa.a: Farhan felt scared, his legs shaking, because Nani said police catch naughty children.

qa.q: What helped Farhan and Uday?
qa.a: Uday remembered that police help lost people, so they approached politely, and the policeman kindly walked them back.

qa.q: How might the policeman have felt when the children asked for help?
qa.a: He seemed amused and kind, laughing gently and happy to help them.

grounding: A child told that police catch naughty children is afraid of the uniform, but learns through a kind officer that police are there to help.

passage:
At the village temple fair, Uma, eight, let go of her mother's hand to watch a puppet show. When she turned, her mother was gone.
She saw a man in khaki near the gate. Her aunt had once warned her, "Misbehave and the police will lock you up." Uma froze and started to cry.
The constable, Omkar, noticed her. He crouched down and took off his cap. "Are you lost, beti? I'm here to help. What's your mother's name?"
Uma sniffled. "Savitri."
He announced it on the loudspeaker. Within minutes, her mother came running.
Before they left, Omkar said, "If you're ever lost, come to someone in this uniform. Speak politely. We help."
Uma waved goodbye to him, still a little shy, but smiling.

qa.q: What was Uma's mother's name?
qa.a: Her mother's name was Savitri.

qa.q: Why did Uma freeze and start to cry?
qa.a: Uma felt frightened, lost at the fair and scared of the police because her aunt had said they would lock her up.

qa.q: What did Omkar do that eased Uma's fear?
qa.a: He crouched down, removed his cap, spoke gently, helped find her mother and explained that she could come to police if lost.

qa.q: How might Uma's mother feel when she found her?
qa.a: Her mother would probably feel hugely relieved and grateful to the constable.

grounding: A child warned that police will lock her up is afraid when lost, and a kind constable shows her police are there to help.

passage: Felix, eight, lived in Hamburg with his Oma, who liked to say, "Behave, or the police will come and take you away." So when a police car stopped outside the bakery, Felix hid behind the flour sacks and would not come out. His friend Oskar tugged at his sleeve. "They're just buying rolls." That week an officer, Frau Becker, visited their class. She let the children try on her cap and explained what to do if they were ever lost: find a police officer or a shop worker, and say your name and street. Felix asked in a tiny voice, "Do you take away bad children?" She crouched down. "No. My job is to help people be safe. You can be careful with people you don't know, and still ask us for help." Felix wore the cap for three whole seconds.

qa.q: Where did Felix hide when the police car stopped?
qa.a: He hid behind the flour sacks.

qa.q: What was Felix feeling when he asked "Do you take away bad children?"
qa.a: Felix was still scared and unsure; his tiny voice shows the fear his Oma's warning had planted.

qa.q: What did Frau Becker do that helped more than a warning?
qa.a: She let the children try the cap, taught them what to do if lost, and explained calmly that police help people be safe while being careful with strangers is fine.

qa.q: Why might Oma have used the police as a threat?
qa.a: Oma probably wanted a quick way to make Felix behave, without realising it would make him afraid of the people meant to help him.

grounding: It illustrates a child frightened of police by an adult's threat, and how a calm explanation that police are there to help, with sensible caution, is healthier.
